meta-description: Every instruction the method gives an AI, in full, as it is actually written.
page-lede: These are the instructions themselves, read straight from the method repository — not a summary of them. Each one says where it is used; open it to read it in full.
layers-note: The instructions are written in English and say what the model should do, never in which language or subject. Three other layers fill the holes they leave open: the language layer, the subject family, and the tree's own file. Sections that come from a layer rather than from the instruction itself are marked.
pickers-note: The language layer and the subject family each have a card of their own further down, with a picker in it. Both choices also decide which marked sections stand inside the instructions above them.
audience-teacher: used by a teacher building a tree
about-keywords: Words in {braces} are filled in when an instruction is composed for one tree. Some come from the tree's own settings, some from the language layer, where a tree can override the default, and the rest from the tree's nodes.
kw-group-language: From the language layer, unless the tree sets it
kw-group-engine: Filled in from the tree's nodes and choices
kw-courseName: The course's name as it reads in a sentence. Setting slots.courseName. No default: without it the braces stay in the text.
kw-motivationSubject: What the motivation dialogue is about, e.g. “maths”. Setting slots.motivationSubject.
kw-expressionFocus: What students in this course get sloppy about when they write. Setting slots.expressionFocus; without it, the section expression is left out.
kw-courseSpecifics: The teacher's own text about the whole course. Setting slots.courseSpecifics; without it, the section courseSpecifics is left out.
kw-conversationLanguage: The language the conversation is held in. A tree can set it with languageName.
kw-learnerDefinite: What the learner is called. A tree chooses with learner (pupil, student or participant), and the language layer gives the word.
kw-examButtonLabel: The label on the tree's test button, so the instruction can point to it.
kw-nodeName: The name of the node the student picked.
kw-nodeDescription: The node's description: what mastering it means.
kw-prerequisiteList: Every node the node or lesson depends on, directly or through others.
kw-aidsText: The tree's text for each aid level that applies, from the settings aids.<n>.*.
kw-nodeCount: How many nodes the test covers.
kw-nodeList: The nodes the student has ticked off, one line each, marked [skill], [concept] or [fact].
kw-taskCount: How many tasks the student asked for.
kw-totalMinutes: The length of the lesson in minutes, chosen by the teacher. How the time is divided is in the section plan, which each subject family writes.
desc-outputLanguage: Specifies the language the conversation is held in, and how to address the student
desc-writingStyle: Examples of the writing advice above in the conversation language
desc-nodeInstruction: The teacher's extra instruction for this node, if the tree has one
fdesc-vocabulary: How to pitch the language and explain new words
fdesc-skillGuidance: How to practise a skill node
fdesc-conceptGuidance: How to test a concept node
fdesc-factGuidance: How to learn and drill a fact node
fdesc-task: How many tasks to make, and what they look like
fdesc-plan: The whole lesson, part by part: starter, each learning goal, diagnostic question and retrieval
desc-extra: The teacher's own additions to this instruction, empty by default
fdesc-starter: The task the lesson begins with
fdesc-examplePair: How each learning goal is taught, round by round
fdesc-argumentsPractice: Arguments for why practice pays off
fdesc-argumentsLongTerm: Arguments for why the subject matters later, used only if the student asks
family-only: No default in this release: only the subject families wrote this section. Choose a family above to read one.
family-none-status: A tree without a subject family gets these default texts. A tree in a subject family gets that family's own version of each.
cond-courseSpecifics: When the tree has a course text
motNoStart: When the student has not said where they are
motStartHard: When the student finds it hard
motStartBored: When the student finds it boring
motStartUse: When the student asks what it is for
miniThreeLevels: When each goal has three levels
miniOneLevel: When each goal has one level
miniMixedTest: When the file ends with a mixed test
miniGame: When the file has game elements
miniEasyRead: When the text is easy to read
miniReadAloud: When the text can be read aloud
simDesignFirst: When the design is agreed first
simBuildNow: When the simulation is built straight away
simTasks: When the simulation comes with tasks
simCritique: When the students criticise the model
cond-lessonIntro: When the lesson type is Introduction
cond-lessonPractice: When the lesson type is Practice
cond-lessonReview: When the lesson type is Review
cond-lessonOther: When the lesson type is Other
fdesc-practiceLanguage: Which language the student practises in
load-failed: The instructions could not be loaded:
about-decomposition: Appended to the authoring prompt below, so that a teacher building a tree hands the model the whole method — the three node types, the data model and the prerequisite rules — before it writes a single row of the file. It is never sent to a student.
about-node: Added to the node a student picks in the tree, and pasted into an AI chat, so that the conversation trains that one skill and nothing else. This is the action the whole tool exists for. It has the model ask questions rather than hand over answers, and say clearly when the skill looks mastered.
about-exam: Added to everything the student has ticked off, from the button at the bottom of a tree, so that the written test spans weeks of work rather than a single node. Spacing and retrieval follow from the design instead of being something the student has to remember to do. It withholds the answers until they have tried.
about-motivation: Added to the subject as a whole, from an optional button a tree can offer, for the student who cannot see why it is worth learning at all. It is a conversation that leads the student to state the value themselves, not a lecture that states it for them — and the tree decides whether to show it.
about-lessonPlan: Added to the part of the tree a teacher selects, so that the lesson plan builds on what the class is assumed to know already. The teacher presses the button on the tree page and takes the result to an AI chat; this is the one instruction here whose reader is a teacher rather than a student.
about-miniTree: Added to the goals a teacher selects, so that a chat model returns one HTML file in which students practise those goals on their own before a test. Laid out like the files of special-education teacher Nina Haugerud: the goals gathered into a few themes with levels, little to read, a worked example before each round, the answer and an explanation after, and mastery that unlocks the next level. The tree decides which goals share a theme and which come first.
about-simulation: Added to the goals a teacher selects, so that a chat model develops a simple interactive simulation of them as one HTML file. After the prompt by Henning Vinjusveen Myhrehagen on skolesim.no: the design is agreed before any code, the subject model governs the simulation, and an "About the model" panel says what it leaves out.
about-authoring: Pasted into an AI chat by a teacher who wants a tree of their own, so that the model asks for the subject, the level and the curriculum and hands back a file this site can read. It wraps the decomposition model above with what the model cannot guess: what the site does with the file, what may be changed, and what each error message means.
about-language: Added to every instruction the engine composes, so that a Norwegian tree is discussed in Norwegian and a Swedish one in Swedish. One file per language holds what the instructions deliberately leave open: which language the conversation is held in, and what good prose looks like in it. The same sections stand marked inside the instructions above, where they land.
about-family: Some sections need different text for different subjects: how to lead in to a topic in mathematics is not how to do it in history. The instructions above refer to this card for those sections. Every subject family has its own version of each of them, copying the default where it has nothing of its own, so two subjects can be compared section by section; “No subject family” shows the defaults, which a tree without a family gets. The same file holds the decomposition rules a teacher or an agent reads before writing a single row of the tree. A tree names its family in its own file.
about-shared: Added to each instruction that names one of these sections, so that text which must read the same everywhere is written once. Kept in one place so the copies cannot drift apart.
versions-note: Every release of the method is here, back to the first. Choosing a version of one instruction moves the whole page to a release that had that version, so the page only shows instructions that were released together. Compare shows each instruction as one table, section by section, with the newer release in the middle column and the older on the right: what was added is green, what was removed is struck through in red.
moved-from: Not in {tag}: there the text was split over {sections}.
format-changed: The format changed between these releases, from Markdown to JSON, so the sections do not line up and the two texts are shown whole, unmarked.
legend-added: text added in the newer release is green
legend-removed: text removed from the older release is struck through in red
